title: A simplified AM1.5 spectrum: irradiance and photon flux
prompt:
The AM1.5 spectrum is approximated by two rectangles:

- $I_{e\lambda} = 1.00$ W m⁻² nm⁻¹ for 250 nm < λ < 1000 nm
- $I_{e\lambda} = 0.25$ W m⁻² nm⁻¹ for 1000 nm < λ < 2000 nm

(a) Calculate the irradiance $I_e$. (b) Calculate the photon flux.

steps.title: Irradiance = area under the spectrum
steps.body:
$I_e = \int I_{e\lambda}\,\mathrm{d}\lambda$, and the area of a rectangle is height × width:

$$I_e = 1.00 \times (1000 - 250) + 0.25 \times (2000 - 1000) = 750 + 250 = 1000\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$$
steps.why: W m⁻² nm⁻¹ × nm = W m⁻²: the nanometres cancel, so no unit conversion is needed in part (a).

steps.title: Photon flux: divide by the photon energy at each wavelength
steps.body:
Each slice $\mathrm{d}\lambda$ contains $I_{e\lambda}\,\mathrm{d}\lambda$ watts, and each photon carries $hc/\lambda$:

$$\Phi = \int \frac{I_{e\lambda}\,\lambda}{hc}\,\mathrm{d}\lambda$$
steps.why: You cannot divide the total 1000 W/m² by one photon energy, because the photon energy is different at every wavelength. That is why the integral is needed.

steps.title: Integrate over each rectangle
steps.body:
With $I_{e\lambda} = P$ constant, $\int_{\lambda_1}^{\lambda_2} \lambda\,\mathrm{d}\lambda = \tfrac{1}{2}(\lambda_2^2 - \lambda_1^2)$, so each band gives

$$\Phi = \frac{P}{2hc}\left(\lambda_2^2 - \lambda_1^2\right)$$
steps.why: This is where the factor 2 comes from: the same 2 as in $\int x\,\mathrm{d}x = x^2/2$.

steps.title: Make the units consistent and compute
steps.why: 1 W m⁻² nm⁻¹ = 10⁹ W m⁻³ and 1 nm² = 10⁻¹⁸ m². Convert both, or keep everything in nm with $hc = 1.986 \times 10^{-16}$ J nm. Mixing the two is off by exactly 10⁹.

steps.title: Add the bands and sanity-check
steps.body:
$\Phi = 2.36 \times 10^{21} + 1.89 \times 10^{21} = 4.25 \times 10^{21}$ m⁻² s⁻¹.

Check: $1000 / (4.25 \times 10^{21}) = 2.35 \times 10^{-19}$ J ≈ 1.47 eV per photon on average, a sensible value for sunlight.

note: The answer book rounds the photon flux to 4.2 × 10²¹ m⁻² s⁻¹; with the formula-sheet constants it is 4.25 × 10²¹.

title: Light entering bare c-Si: refraction, reflection and trapping
prompt:
Cell A is a 100 µm thick c-Si layer with a flat front and a rear reflector. λ = 1000 nm, $n = 3.57$ (ignore κ).

(a) Find $\theta_t$ for $\theta_i$ = 0°, 30°, 60°, 90°. (b) Find the unpolarised reflectance $R$ for those angles. (c) How far does the light travel to the reflector? (d) The rear reflector sends all light up at a fixed angle $\theta_{\mathrm{BR}}$. Which $\theta_{\mathrm{BR}}$ guarantees total internal reflection at the front?

steps.title: (a) Snell’s law with n₁ = 1.0, n₂ = 3.57
steps.why: Entering a much denser medium, the ray bends strongly towards the normal. Even grazing light (90°) ends up within 16.3° of the normal inside the silicon.

steps.title: (b) Fresnel equations, then average
steps.why: At 0° all cosines are 1 and you can use the short formula $R = \left(\frac{1 - 3.57}{1 + 3.57}\right)^2 = 0.316$. Square the amplitude coefficients; sunlight is half s, half p.

steps.title: (c) Path length uses the angle inside the silicon
steps.body:
From the geometry, $d = t/\cos\theta_t$ with $t = 100$ µm:

- 0° → 100 µm, 30° → 101 µm, 60° → 103 µm, 90° → 104 µm
steps.why: Use $\theta_t$, not $\theta_i$: the ray travels through the silicon at the refracted angle. Because $\theta_t$ is always small, the path barely changes.

steps.title: (d) Critical angle at the c-Si/air interface
steps.body:
Front and back are parallel, so the ray reaches the front at $\theta_{\mathrm{BR}}$. TIR requires $\theta_{\mathrm{BR}} > \theta_{\mathrm{crit}}$ with (eq. 4.19)

$$\sin\theta_{\mathrm{crit}} = \frac{1.0}{3.57} \Rightarrow \theta_{\mathrm{crit}} = 16.3°$$
steps.why: A normal mirror would send the light back inside the escape cone (it entered at at most 16.3°), so it would leave again. The special reflector aims everything outside the cone.

note: The official answer gives R = 31.7 % (30°) and 32.4 % (60°): it averages the already-rounded $r_p^2$ and $r_s^2$. Unrounded values give 31.6 % and 32.3 %. Both are accepted at exam precision.

title: Choosing an anti-reflective coating
prompt:
Cell B is cell A with a non-absorbing coating: MgF₂ (n = 1.38), ITO (n = 1.87) or TiO₂ (n = 2.49). Normal incidence.

(e) Calculate $R_1$ (air/coating) and $R_2$ (coating/c-Si) for each. (f) Which gives the lowest $R_{\mathrm{tot}} = R_1 + R_2$? Compare with cell A (no multiple reflections or interference). (g) Which $\theta_{\mathrm{BR}}$ is needed for TIR at the coating/air interface? Higher or lower than for cell A, and why?

steps.title: (e) Normal-incidence reflectance at each interface
steps.why: The question says 0°, so use the short formula. The order of $n_1$, $n_2$ doesn’t matter because the difference is squared.

steps.title: (f) Add and compare
steps.body: $R_{\mathrm{tot}}$: MgF₂ 22.1 %, **ITO 19.0 %**, TiO₂ 21.4 %. Bare c-Si (cell A): 31.6 %. ITO is best.
steps.why: A low-index coating makes $R_1$ small but $R_2$ big, and vice versa. The best single layer has $n_c = \sqrt{n_0 n_s} = \sqrt{3.57} = 1.89$ (eq. 10.32), and ITO’s 1.87 is closest.

steps.title: Bonus (official answer ‘g’): quarter-wave thickness
steps.body:
For destructive interference at 1000 nm: $d = \lambda_0/(4 n_c)$ (eq. 10.38):

- MgF₂: 181 nm, ITO: 134 nm, TiO₂: 100 nm
steps.why: The official answer sheet includes this as part ‘g’, although no question asks for it. It is good exam practice anyway.

steps.title: (g) TIR threshold with a coating
steps.body:
1. Critical angle at coating/air: $\sin\theta_c = 1/n_c$ (e.g. MgF₂: 46.4°).
2. Angle in the c-Si that refracts into the coating at exactly that angle: $3.57\sin\theta_{\mathrm{BR}} = n_c\sin\theta_c = 1$.

So $\theta_{\mathrm{BR}} = \arcsin(1/3.57) = 16.3°$ for every coating: the same as for cell A.
steps.why: Snell’s law through parallel layers: $n_{\mathrm{Si}}\sin\theta_{\mathrm{BR}} = n_c\sin\theta_c = n_{\mathrm{air}}\sin 90°$. The middle term only links the two ends, so the coating index cancels.

answer: (e) see table; (f) ITO, $R_{\mathrm{tot}} = 19.0\,\%$ vs 31.6 % without coating; (g) $\theta_{\mathrm{BR}} > 16.3°$, identical to cell A, because $n\sin\theta$ is conserved through parallel layers.
note: Official answer lettering is shifted: its ‘g’ (coating thickness) answers no question and its ‘h’ answers question (g). This example follows the question letters.

title: LEDs, reflection losses and photocurrent in a tandem
prompt:
Three monochromatic LEDs: X (500 nm, 380 W/m²), Y (1000 nm, 400 W/m²), Z (1300 nm, 220 W/m²). Cell A: $E_G = 1.70$ eV, $n = 2.5$. Cell B: $E_G = 1.12$ eV, $n = 4.0$. In the tandem, A sits on B, glued with EVA ($n = 1.5$). Interfaces: R₁ air/A, R₂ air/B, R₃ A/EVA, R₄ EVA/B. Normal incidence, ignore κ; cells absorb all photons above their gap and none below.

(a) Photon flux density of each LED. (b) R₁…R₄. (c) $J_{\mathrm{ph}}$ for: 1. cell A alone, 2. cell B alone, 3. tandem A + B.

steps.title: (a) Photon flux = irradiance / photon energy
steps.why: Monochromatic light: no integral. Y gives more photons than X for almost the same power, because each of its photons carries half the energy.

steps.title: Decide per photon, per cell: is E ≥ E_G?
steps.body:
- X (2.48 eV): above both gaps → absorbed by whichever cell it reaches first
- Y (1.24 eV): below A’s 1.70 eV, above B’s 1.12 eV → passes A, absorbed in B
- Z (0.95 eV): below both → never absorbed
steps.why: Do this before any arithmetic: it tells you which fluxes enter each current.

steps.title: (c) Experiments 1 and 2: one interface each
steps.body:
$J_{\mathrm{ph}} = q\,\Phi_{\mathrm{abs}}$, one electron per absorbed photon.

1. Cell A: $(1 - R_1)\Phi_X = 0.816 \times 9.57 \times 10^{20} = 7.81 \times 10^{20}$ → $J = 125$ A/m²
2. Cell B: $(1 - R_2)(\Phi_X + \Phi_Y) = 0.640 \times 2.97 \times 10^{21} = 1.90 \times 10^{21}$ → $J = 305$ A/m²
steps.why: State the assumption ‘one electron per absorbed photon’ in your answer: the question doesn’t say it outright.

steps.title: (c) Experiment 3: list the interfaces before multiplying
steps.body:
Top cell A still gets X through $R_1$: $J_A = 125$ A/m².

Y passes A and reaches B through $R_1$, $R_3$ and $R_4$:

$$(1 - R_1)(1 - R_3)(1 - R_4)\,\Phi_Y = 0.816 \times 0.9375 \times 0.793 \times 2.01 \times 10^{21} = 1.22 \times 10^{21}$$

$J_B = q \times 1.22 \times 10^{21} = 196$ A/m².
steps.why: Each interface removes a fraction of what reaches it, so the transmitted fractions multiply. $R_2$ does not appear: it belongs to experiment 2, where B is lit directly.

note: The official answers use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴, c = 3 × 10⁸ and q = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹, hence slightly lower currents (124.6, 302.6, 194.4 A/m²). The marking scheme: (a) 5 pts, (b) 4 pts, (c) 6 pts. The cell-B lines in the official answer are labelled ‘q·φ_ph,X’ but use the correct fluxes.
